section.title: Careers
section.intro: What the work is actually like, and how people get into it. Every job here has more than one way in, even if the person doing it only took one of them.

items.title: Electrician
items.subtitle: Trades
items.summary: Get paid from your first year with no fees, and be fully qualified in about four. After that you can work for a company or for yourself.
items.body:
Electricians install and repair electrical systems in houses, building sites and factories. More and more, that includes solar panels, heat pumps and car chargers. It's a skilled trade with a formal qualification at the end, and people do fail the exams. Don't let anyone tell you it's unskilled work.

Once you're qualified you can work for a company, set up on your own, or move up to running sites.

routes.name: Apprenticeship
routes.detail: Find an employer who'll register you, then you alternate between working for them and blocks of training. You're paid the whole way through.

routes.name: PLC first, then apprenticeship
routes.tag: If you can't find an employer yet
routes.detail: A year of electrical training makes employers far more likely to take you on. It's a common route if you finish sixth year without anything lined up.

routes.name: Later on
routes.detail: Some people start at twenty-eight after five years in a job they didn't enjoy, and that's completely normal.

blocks.heading: What you need
blocks.text: A Leaving Cert at a basic grade, or an approved equivalent, or an employer who wants to take you on anyway. Maths and a practical subject help, but high points aren't what matters here. Entry requirements change, so check the current ones before you rely on this.

blocks.heading: What you earn on the way
blocks.text: You're paid a percentage of the qualified rate from year one, and it goes up each year. By the end you've been paid for four years and you owe nothing, which is worth comparing honestly with the college route.

myths.myth: It's what you do if you're not academic.
myths.reality: People fail the exams every year. It's a different kind of difficult, not an easier one.
It helps, which is why this site exists. Ringing local firms yourself also works, and hardly anyone does it, which works in your favour.
There's plenty. Electricians move into supervision, contracting, inspection and teaching, or run their own company, and some earn more than people with degrees.

items.title: Software developer
items.subtitle: Technology
items.summary: A well-paid job where, after your first role, people care far more about what you can build than where you studied.
items.body:
Developers write the code behind apps and systems. It's more of a team job than people think. A lot of the day goes on reading other people's code, agreeing what to build, and fixing things that worked yesterday.

Ireland has far more of this work than you'd expect for its size. There are the big multinationals, and plenty of Irish companies you've probably never heard of.

routes.name: Computer science degree
routes.detail: Three or four years through the CAO. It gives you the strongest grounding, and it's the easiest way onto the graduate programmes the bigger companies hire through.
routes.cost: Student contribution, often covered by SUSI

routes.name: Apprenticeship
routes.detail: Software and ICT apprenticeships exist in Ireland, but they don't get talked about much. You work and study at the same time, and finish with a qualification and real work experience.

routes.name: PLC, then work or a degree
routes.detail: A computing course in further education can lead straight into junior roles, or on to a degree through links with the universities.

routes.name: Teaching yourself
routes.detail: It does happen, and this industry cares more about what you can build than where you studied. But there's no structure and no one to ask, and you need finished projects to show. It works better as a second career than as a first job.

blocks.heading: What you need
blocks.text: Points for computing courses vary a lot, and there are good options well below the top. Maths helps and some courses need it, but it's less of a barrier than people think. Apprenticeships and further education ask for a lot less. Check the entry requirements for the specific course.

blocks.heading: What it pays
blocks.text: Starting salaries in tech are high compared with most first jobs in Ireland, and they rise quickly in the first few years. The apprenticeship route pays you from day one.

myths.myth: You need to have been coding since you were twelve.
myths.reality: Plenty of developers started at eighteen, or thirty. Starting early helps, but it isn't a requirement.
Some courses want it, many don't, and most day-to-day work uses very little of it.

myths.myth: It has to be a well-known university.
myths.reality: After your first job, hardly anyone asks. What you've built matters far more.
